correctness.rationale: An inscribed triangle has area at most 3√3/4, with equality only for an equilateral triple on a great circle. The zero vector sum at equality and nonnegative heights force all three heights to zero. Compactness gives localization to the two labelled orientation circles. The Gram expansion gives angular coefficient √3/4 and altitude term (√3/12)(z1+z2+z3)^2. Although the altitude Hessian has rank one, on the positive octant the square of the sum dominates the sum of squares. Uniform smooth-chart remainders can therefore be absorbed, confining every scaled event to a common bounded region. The scaled indicators converge off a null boundary, giving both the volume asymptotic and L1 convergence of the normalized densities. The angular matrix has determinant 9/64; the vertical simplex radial density is S^2/2. The five-volume is 64π·3^(3/4)/45, and uniform surface density with both orientations and the phase contributes 1/(2π²). In the limit, J has density proportional to J^(1/2)(1-J), the simplex proportions and whitened rescaled disk coordinate are independent of J and each other, and homogeneity yields the Beta(5/2,1) deficit law. Rotation and reflection give the asserted phase and orientation factors.
residual_risks: The total variation statement is for the rescaled configuration in the specified charts; convergence of the actual normalized deficit follows from the uniform remainder and continuity of the limiting distribution. Numerical finite-threshold checks are corroborative only.

evidence: Akopyan–Edelsbrunner–Nikitenko Lemma 5 gives radius–shape independence for the full sphere; it does not incorporate the hemisphere orientation constraints. Bárány et al. broader_coverage.reasoning: General spherical integration formulas can enable an alternative derivation but one still needs the shrinking orientation feasible region at the great-circle optimizer and its correct coupling with heights. Full-sphere size–shape independence alone does not give that conditioning or the geometric marks.

evidence: Projection gives a beta-like radial density on a planar disk, but with just one altitude z nonzero at the equilateral phases the projected deficit is (√3/4)z², versus (√3/12)z² for chord area. In three heights the quadratic forms differ by more than an overall reparameterization: the chord vertical term has mixed products.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The same endpoint and exponent of a projected-area theorem would not determine the coefficient or conditional marks of chord area. Conditioning a full-sphere theorem also requires a configuration-dependent orientation probability, not a universal factor of 1/8 on the extreme event.

value.rationale: The hemisphere is a natural boundary-pinned geometry. The quadratic form is degenerate in unrestricted tilt directions yet controls all allowed heights on the positive cone; this explains the exponent and yields a concrete sharp coefficient and independent shape marks. The chord/projection distinction is quantitatively meaningful even though the two areas share the extremizer.
